ARC Robotics
University teams design and build robots for tactical arena matches. Robots drive, aim and fire projectiles at opponents’ armour panels to reduce their hit points.
Formerly RoboMaster North America, ARC offers
1v1
, 
3v3

.

ARC has an established field of university teams, including Purdue, NYU, McMaster, Queen’s, Ontario Tech and UBC.

1v1 Infantry
One robot and one pilot; two-minute rounds.
Keeps first-season integration manageable by focusing the team on one complete robot.
2026–2027 season

Our projectile exceeds a published eye-injury benchmark
Assessment
Finding and resulting decision
1. Projectile energy
Our 3.2 g, 17 mm projectile carries 1 joule at the 25 m/s limit.
Dividing by its frontal area gives approximately 0.44 J/cm².
This lets us compare the shot with published eye-impact research.
2. Injury benchmark
Duma et al. (2005) modelled eye injury using energy per projected area.
Their 50% corneal-abrasion benchmark was approximately 0.15 J/cm².
Corneal abrasion is damage to the eye’s clear front surface.
3. Implication for us
Our 0.44 J/cm² is roughly three times that benchmark.
This supports treating direct eye impact as an injury hazard.
4. Contain the shots
Use UTRA Combat’s wooden box after confirming its walls, lid and gaps contain shots.
No separate body armour is proposed for fully enclosed tests
Any Testing outside the box will require that everyone is wearing adequate eye protection
5. Train, protect
and control
Every member must complete UTRA-required safety training before hands-on work.
Wear impact-rated goggles; verify shot speed stays within 25 m/s.
Keep an emergency stop accessible and disable firing whenever the box is open.
Before access: unload, disconnect power and wait for moving parts to stop.
AH
